### Reviewer 3

The paper "Tandem Bulk Oxygen Diffusion and Surface Reactions in Reducible Metal Oxides Control Redox
Cycle Dynamics" describes a study of oxygen mobility and surface reactions in ceria–zirconia catalysts. Using transient kinetics, in
situ spectroscopies, and machine-learning–based molecular dynamics simulations, the authors uncover complex, reduction-
dependent oxygen diffusion mechanisms. They find that oxygen mobility is highest at intermediate reduction levels due to a
balance between oxygen vacancies and lattice distortions, while different defect types dominate at low and high reductions,
challenging conclusions drawn from isotope exchange experiments. The results show that surface oxygen is continuously
replenished, making hydrogen dissociation the rate-limiting step, and suggest that catalysts can exhibit spatially varying
oxidation states. The paper addresses a relevant problem and reports a methodology that is broadly applicable to other
reducible oxide materials. In this respect, the work presented is definitely at the level required for publication in Nature
Communications.
Given my background in electronic structure theory, I will restrict my comments to this aspect of the work. The authors have
performed molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learning potential to investigate oxygen diffusion processes,
interactions with H₂, and water desorption leading to reduced samples. Particularly commendable is the use of state-of-the-
art electronic structure methods, such as DFT+U and the hybrid HSE06 functional. This level of theory is essential, as the
reduction of ceria involves the formation of localized Ce³⁺ polarons that cannot be properly described using semilocal
functionals. Overall, the computational work is of high quality and provides a valuable and necessary complement to the
experimental observations.
There are, however, two aspects that warrant further consideration. First, the analysis of H₂ reaction and H₂O desorption is
based exclusively on the CZO (111) facet. This choice is reasonable given that the average particle size is approximately 30
nm. Nonetheless, even particles of this size can exhibit surface defects and low-coordinated sites, whose influence
becomes increasingly important as particle size decreases. It has been shown that small zirconia nanoparticles behave
quite differently from extended zirconia surfaces with respect to H₂ dissociation and water desorption. In particular, while
heterolytic H₂ splitting (Zr–H⁻/O–H⁺) is energetically favored on extended surfaces, homolytic splitting, leading to the
formation of two OH groups and the transfer of two electrons to Zr³⁺ sites, becomes preferred on zirconia
nanoparticles. Similarly, H₂O desorption is favored over O₂ desorption on ZrO₂ nanoparticles, in contrast to extended surfaces (see
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b05984 and https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.7b00799). In light of these findings, it would
be appropriate to include a discussion of the potential role of surface defects and nanoparticle size in shaping the observed
kinetic behavior.
The second point is more exploratory in nature. The authors consider a wide range of reduction levels for the CZO
nanoparticles, up to 50%. The discussion, however, focuses primarily on kinetics, particularly on the relative diffusion
barriers. It would be interesting to address the accompanying changes in the electronic structure. To what extent are the
excess electrons localized, and how does their degree of localization evolve with increasing reduction? What is the
electronic nature of highly reduced CZO particles? While one may expect strongly reduced ceria–zirconia to exhibit
increased electronic conductivity, it remains unclear whether the system retains an insulating or semiconductor with
polaronic character, or whether it approaches metallic behavior. Given the level of theory employed, the existing
computational results should enable the authors to at least qualitatively address this question.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript presents a comprehensive and compelling study that integrates experiments and MLP-based MD
simulations to unravel the complex interplay between oxygen diffusion and surface reactions during the reduction of CZO.
The application of MLP-based MD overcomes the significant limitations of experimental techniques and conventional DFT
calculations. The key finding is that the optimal oxygen mobility occurs at intermediate reduction levels due to a trade-off
between vacancy availability and lattice distortion, providing atomic insights to redox kinetics. In summary, this work is of
high quality and well supported by data. However, this paper is probably published, but revision is needed.
1. The force threshold for structural optimization is only 0.05 eV/Å in the present DFT study, while this value is usually
suggested as 0.01~0.02 eV/Å. Why did the authors use a lower convergence here? Will it bring any unconvergent energetic
results?
2. More details of the MLP should be provided. For example, how to construct the training set and testing set? What is the
number of training set? What kind of machine learning model was used? What is the parameter setting in the ML model?
3. Figure S7 only demonstrates a general picture for energy and force accuracy. However, whether the MLP can accurately
describe the energy profile of Vo diffusion identical to NEB result using DFT should be demonstrated. Other details of the
MLP performance (e.g., R2 values of training set and testing set data, and so on) should also be provided.
4. The active learning loop is terminated when the extrapolation grades of all structures are less than 2 during 1-ns
simulation, however, the MLP-based MD simulations are performed in NVT for 10 ns. How to guarantee the accuracy of MD
